title: A proof that an explicit one-way function exists

concept.text: The innovation would be an unconditional mathematical proof that a fully specified function is easy to compute but computationally hard to reverse on average. Given an output produced from a uniformly random input, an efficient attacker should have only negligible probability of finding any input that produces that output. Finding a different valid preimage would count as successful inversion; recovering the original input is not required. The intended guarantee concerns growing input lengths and computational resources, rather than a fixed puzzle that has resisted attacks.

The missing object is a proof of one-wayness, rather than another candidate function. An explicit universal function is already documented that is one-way if and only if any one-way function exists. Its explicit description therefore does not settle existence: the unresolved step is proving that efficient inversion really is impossible. Proving this universal function one-way would qualify, as would proving another explicit polynomial-time function one-way in the stated security model.

significance.text: An unconditional proof would establish a foundational existence theorem for classical computational cryptography. One-way functions imply pseudorandom generators, private-key encryption, message authentication codes, and digital signatures. Their existence would also imply P ≠ NP, connecting an average-case cryptographic hardness result to a central separation in computational complexity. These consequences make the proposed advance revolutionary at the level of mathematical foundations.

The immediate consequence would be the provable existence of these primitives with asymptotic security. It would not automatically supply efficient constructions, useful concrete security parameters, or a security proof for deployed implementations. A tight proof for AES would require additional results connecting that particular construction and its parameters to a proven hardness statement. Likewise, classical one-wayness alone would not establish resistance to quantum attackers.

Standard public-key encryption is a separate ambition. The documented generic consequences of one-way functions do not establish it, so this innovation would not by itself resolve CRY-02. Brzuska and Couteau distinguish the cryptographic world supported by one-way functions from stronger public-key capabilities; their discussion of weaker public-key consequences under exponential hardness does not close that gap.

Conditional downstream possibility: if the proof also yielded efficient constructions and meaningful concrete bounds, it could support practical cryptography whose foundational hardness no longer rests on an unproved assumption. That practical outcome would depend on the construction, reduction losses, implementation, and adversary model. It is a possible extension of the foundational result, rather than an automatic consequence of existence alone.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability is proving average-case inversion hardness for an explicit efficiently computable function. Worst-case difficulty is insufficient: a function could have a few exceptionally difficult inputs while being easy to invert on almost every input encountered by the security experiment. A successful argument must establish the required inversion bound over the specified random-input distribution against every adversary covered by its model. P ≠ NP would be a consequence of one-way functions, but it is not known to be sufficient to establish their existence.

Even assuming general average-case hardness for NP problems has not supplied the missing construction. The reviewed paper explains that a construction of one-way functions from general average-case hard NP problems must use non-relativizing techniques. This is a barrier to that route: a proof cannot simply carry through unchanged in every oracle setting. It does not establish that every possible unconditional proof of one-way functions must take the same form or overcome precisely the same barrier.

A more specific route concerns time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity, which measures how briefly a string can be described by a program subject to a running-time bound. Brzuska and Couteau report that the Liu–Pass theorem makes mild average-case hardness of computing this quantity sufficient for the existence of one-way functions. The missing step along this route would be an unconditional proof of the required hardness under the theorem's precise hypotheses. The supplied review does not establish all parameters or whether the resulting guarantee meets the proposed nonuniform adversary criterion.

current_state.text: The retained Wikipedia article reports the existence of one-way functions as an open conjecture, describes the explicit universal function, and records the implication to P ≠ NP. It provides a secondary overview rather than a primary proof. The supplied materials document candidates and conditional implications; they do not provide an unconditional proof of classical one-way functions.

Chris Brzuska and Geoffroy Couteau's “On Building Fine-Grained One-Way Functions from Strong Average-Case Hardness,” published online on December 4, 2024, in Journal of Cryptology, establishes two distinct negative results. One is an oracle separation from exponential average-case NP hardness, ruling out relativizing reductions in that setting. The other is a black-box separation from exponentially self-amplifiable average-case hardness. These are different restrictions on possible constructions and reductions; they should not both be described as full oracle separations.

The paper explicitly describes the two negative results as incomparable. For the self-amplifiable-hardness setting, it explains that obtaining a full oracle separation would require additional access for the construction and leaves embedding the adversary into the oracle open. These results constrain routes from strong average-case assumptions to fine-grained one-way functions; they neither prove that one-way functions cannot exist nor supply an unconditional existence proof.

The supplied evidence has limits that matter to the scope of this account. The Wikipedia extraction was complete, and the review reports an August 2026 edit, but the supplied search record contains no independent freshness check through November 1, 2026. The paper's retained HTML stops in Section 6.5, and its PDF extraction stops during page 51 of 70. The reviewed introduction and relevant passages support the dated findings and distinctions above; the remaining text was not fully available in those extractions. These limitations do not invalidate the documented results, but they prevent an exhaustive claim about all subsequent work or every practical cipher.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed completion criterion: a publicly checkable, unconditional proof that a named polynomial-time function has negligible inversion success against every nonuniform polynomial-size circuit family, when its outputs are generated from uniformly random inputs. The proof should specify input and output lengths, the security parameter, and what constitutes a valid preimage. Negligible success means that the inversion probability eventually falls below every inverse-polynomial bound as the security parameter grows. Nonuniform circuit security is a chosen strengthening for this record, rather than a consensus completion rule established by the supplied sources.
completion_criteria.label: Unconditional proof establishes negligible inversion against nonuniform polynomial-size circuits

completion_criteria.text: Proving the documented universal function one-way in that model would meet the proposed criterion. Alternatively, an unconditional hardness theorem for time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity could qualify through the Liu–Pass implication, provided its exact hypotheses and conclusion were checked and shown to deliver the required adversary model. The reviewed summary supports this route in principle but does not settle that model compatibility.
completion_criteria.label: Universal-function or Liu–Pass proof delivers the required adversary model

completion_criteria.text: Proposed verification process: independent experts should be able to reconstruct the argument, check every reduction and quantifier, and verify that no unproved hardness assumption remains. Formal verification could strengthen confidence but is not proposed as mandatory. Implementations, challenge instances, and attack experiments could check examples and practical behavior; finite tests cannot establish an asymptotic guarantee against every efficient inverter.
completion_criteria.label: Experts reconstruct proof and exclude all unproved hardness assumptions

completion_criteria.text: Proposed scope boundary: classical security alone would constitute the foundational breakthrough. Security against quantum polynomial-time inverters would be a further strengthening requiring an explicitly stated quantum adversary model. Practical deployment should be assessed separately through concrete security bounds, computation and storage costs, and implementation evidence; an existence proof need not meet those additional engineering goals.
completion_criteria.label: Stronger: Quantum security holds under an explicit quantum adversary model

related_concepts.text: CRY-02, “Public-key encryption from one-way functions,” asks for a further implication beyond CRY-01's existence proof. CRY-01 would establish a minimal foundation for major classical cryptographic primitives; CRY-02 would connect that foundation to standard public-key encryption. Resolving either question does not, by its stated scope alone, resolve the other: a conditional construction from one-way functions could still leave their unconditional existence open.

Roster-based synthesis: CRY-03, “Practically efficient post-quantum indistinguishability obfuscation,” and CRY-04, “General-purpose private computation at near-plaintext cost,” concern stronger functionality and practical efficiency. They overlap with CRY-01 in seeking rigorous computational security, but neither capability nor its performance target follows from the existence theorem described here. CRY-01 also does not automatically supply their quantum security requirements.

Roster-based synthesis: CRY-05, “Publicly verifiable unclonable money and copy-protected programs,” CRY-06, “Practical classical verification of quantum computation,” and CRY-07, “Position verification that works in physical spacetime,” concern distinct operational guarantees involving copying, quantum computation, or physical location. Their relationship to CRY-01 is a shared interest in provable security under an explicit adversary model. The supplied evidence establishes no general reduction from classical one-way functions to those full capabilities.

Roster-based synthesis: CRY-08, “Metadata-private messaging at ordinary cost,” adds communication privacy and system cost requirements beyond the existence of encryption primitives. CRY-09, “Post-quantum timed release with a sequentiality theorem,” adds quantum resistance and a guarantee about unavoidable sequential computation. Average-case difficulty of inversion alone does not establish either system-level metadata protection or the required timed-release behavior.

Roster-based synthesis: CRY-10, “A conclusive quantum classification of deployed lattice encryption,” concerns particular deployed schemes and quantum attacks. CRY-01 concerns unconditional existence and can be completed with a classical security result for a function having no immediate deployment use. A quantum classification of lattice encryption would therefore answer a different question from proving that some classical one-way function exists.

brief.title: A proof that some calculations are hard to undo
possible: People could rely on a mathematical proof that some calculations are easy to do but hard to undo. Such a calculation is called a one-way function. Even finding a different input that produces the same output would count as undoing it. The protection would apply to randomly chosen inputs as their length grows.
why: Cryptographers would gain a proved foundation for secret-key encryption, digital signatures, and checks that messages are authentic. The existence of these tools would no longer depend on an unproved assumption about computational difficulty.

sources.showed: This overview explains that one-way functions remain unproved. It describes a fully specified universal function that is one-way if any one-way function exists.
sources.quote:
There is an explicit function
f
that has been proved to be one-way, if and only if one-way functions exist.
sources.cited_for: A specific function is already known whose one-wayness would settle existence.
sources.not_established: The universal function has not been proved hard to reverse.

sources.showed: They built functions with a limited gap between computation and reversal costs under a strong hardness assumption. They also proved distinct barriers to approaches using weaker assumptions.
sources.quote:
We show that if there is an
\(\textsf{NP} \)
language having a very strong form of average-case hardness, which we call
block finding hardness
, then FGOWF exist.
sources.cited_for: Strong assumptions can support weaker forms of one-wayness, but some routes from computational difficulty face proven barriers.
sources.not_established: The construction remains conditional and does not establish the full reversal resistance required here.

shown: A fully specified universal function is known, but its resistance to reversal remains unproved. Brzuska and Couteau established conditional constructions with weaker protection and barriers to certain proof methods. An unconditional existence proof remains missing.
missing: A proof must establish difficulty across randomly chosen inputs; a few exceptionally hard cases would not suffice.
The proof must defeat every attacker allowed by its stated model without relying on an unproved hardness assumption.
Practical encryption would also need usable security bounds, efficient constructions, and implementation evidence.

milestones.label: Reversal success below every inverse power of input length
milestones.explanation: An unconditional proof must establish this for a named efficient function against circuits tailored to each length, with size bounded by a fixed power of that length. This would prove one-wayness on uniformly random inputs.

milestones.label: A known route delivers the required attacker protection
milestones.explanation: The universal function, or the Liu–Pass route through hardness of finding shortest programs under a time limit, must deliver the required protection. Either could establish existence if its precise conditions hold.

milestones.label: Independent experts reconstruct the proof without unproved assumptions
milestones.explanation: Independent experts must reconstruct the argument and confirm that no unproved hardness assumption remains. This would establish confidence beyond attack experiments, which cannot prove protection as inputs grow.

milestones.label: Further protection against quantum attackers
milestones.explanation: A stronger proof would establish resistance to efficient quantum attacks under an explicit model of their capabilities. This would extend the classical result to quantum attackers.

uncertain: It remains unclear whether the Liu–Pass route delivers protection against circuits tailored separately to each input length.
Requiring protection against such circuits is a proposed completion standard, rather than an established consensus.
Classical one-wayness alone would not establish quantum resistance or the security of deployed encryption.

page.title: Unconditional existence of one-way functions
page.definition: An explicit function on bit strings would be computable in polynomial time and provably hard to reverse without a hardness assumption. Given the output for a uniformly random n-bit input and the length n, any uniform classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm would have probability below n^(−c) of finding any input with that output, for every fixed c>0 and all sufficiently large n. Modular exponentiation illustrates the gap: computing the power is efficient, while the required hardness of recovering an exponent remains conjectural.

goal.need: People use shared keys to keep messages private and digital signatures to check who signed data and whether it was altered. Secure schemes for both tasks, along with pseudorandom generators, pseudorandom functions and commitments, depend on a common conjecture. A proof would establish that all five are possible against efficient classical attackers. If one-way functions do not exist, none of the five can meet its standard computational security definition. Public-key encryption lies outside this equivalence.

statements.quote: OWFs are vital components of modern symmetric encryptions, digital signatures, authentic schemes and more.
Internet security today relies on cryptographic constructions based on the *conjectured* hardness of some computational problems
statements.context: From the objective of grant 101142322, signed on 30 April 2024. The project studies cryptographic hardness assumptions.

completion.title: An unconditional proof establishes negligible inversion probability for an explicit one-way function.
completion.criterion: An unconditional proof establishes a fully specified deterministic polynomial-time function f:{0,1}*→{0,1}*. For every uniform classical probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm A and every c>0, Pr[f(A(1^n,f(x)))=f(x)]<n^(−c) for all sufficiently large n. Here x is uniform on {0,1}^n, probability includes A’s randomness, and 1^n supplies the input length in unary. Finding any preimage counts as success.
completion.set_by: Cryptographic community convention, stated by Liu and Pass in ITCS 2026, Section 2.1, Definition 2.1.
completion.threshold_quote: no probabilistic polynomial-time ($\mathrm{𝖯𝖯𝖳}$) algorithm can invert $f$ with inverse polynomial probability for infinitely many input lengths $n$.
completion.basis: Definition 2.1 gives the uniform security test. Theorem 2.3 equates weak and strong existence by amplification. Existence remains open.

milestones.title: An explicit polynomial-time function is one-way if and only if any one-way function exists.
milestones.criterion: Specify a deterministic polynomial-time function f and prove that if any one-way function exists, then f is one-way. Here one-wayness requires negligible success for every uniform classical probabilistic polynomial-time inverter on outputs of uniformly random inputs. The reverse implication follows by taking f itself as the witness to existence.
milestones.set_by: The field’s completeness criterion for one-way functions, established for Tiling Expansion by Levin, Section 4.3, Theorem 1.
milestones.threshold_quote: Tiling Expansion is a owf if and only if owfs exist.

milestones.title: A random-language-model function distribution has negligible inversion below T^(2−ε), at evaluation cost T.
milestones.criterion: For each fixed 0<ε<1, exhibit a function distribution D in the random language model with security parameter λ=2^n. At every sufficiently large input length m, consider any oracle circuit of size below T_f(m)^(2−ε) for every f in the support of D, where T_f(m) is the evaluation circuit’s wire count. Given f, f(z) and 1^m, the circuit must find a preimage with probability negligible in λ over the model’s random function and uniform m-bit input z. The model checks membership claims using hidden random witnesses.
milestones.set_by: Brzuska and Couteau’s published fine-grained one-way-function criterion, Definition 7 and Corollary 26, in the random language model.
milestones.threshold_quote: For any \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists a \((\textsf{negl}(\lambda ), 1-\varepsilon )\)-fine-grained one-way function distribution in the random language model.

milestones.title: An explicit function has negligible inversion probability at infinitely many input lengths.
milestones.criterion: Prove unconditionally that an explicit deterministic polynomial-time function f has the following property. For every uniform classical probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm A, there are a negligible function μ_A and an infinite set of lengths S_A such that Pr[f(A(1^n,f(x)))=f(x)]≤μ_A(n) for every n in S_A. The probability is over a uniform n-bit input x and the random choices of A. The set S_A may depend on A.
milestones.set_by: The field’s infinitely-often one-wayness convention, stated by Liu and Pass, CRYPTO 2021, Section 2.1, Definition 1.
milestones.threshold_quote: holds for infinitely many n ∈ N (as opposed to all).

milestones.title: One-way function existence is equivalent to mild average-case hardness of computing Kᵗ.
milestones.criterion: For every constant ε>0 and polynomial time bound t(n)≥(1+ε)n, prove the following equivalence. One-way functions exist if and only if some positive polynomial p satisfies this condition: for every uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm A and all sufficiently large n, Pr[A(x)≠Kᵗ(x)]≥1/p(n). Here x is uniform on n-bit strings, probability includes A’s randomness, and Kᵗ(x) is the length of the shortest program that outputs x within t(n) steps on the fixed universal machine.
milestones.set_by: Liu and Pass’s average-case characterization, Theorem 1.1 and its strengthened form, recognized by the NSA’s 2022 paper competition.
milestones.threshold_quote: mild average-case hardness of $K^{t}$ is equivalent to the existence of one-way functions.

not_found: No externally prescribed sequence of milestones for an unconditional one-way-function proof was found.
No accepted unconditional existence proof was found, including for infinitely-often one-way functions.
No academy, prize committee or research programme statement explicitly setting an unconditional existence proof as its goal was found.
No academy, prize committee or research programme statement disputing the value or feasibility of an unconditional proof was found.

results.finding: Levin’s theorem identifies one explicit universal function that is one-way whenever any one-way function exists.
results.quote:
There is an explicit function
f
that has been proved to be one-way, if and only if one-way functions exist.

results.finding: The article reports both directions of the equivalence between one-way function existence and mild average-case hardness of time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity.
results.detail: The supplied text cites an arXiv preprint for this result.
results.quote:
There also exists a function that is one-way if polynomial-time bounded
Kolmogorov complexity
is mildly hard on average. Since the existence of one-way functions implies that polynomial-time bounded Kolmogorov complexity is mildly hard on average, the function is a universal one-way function.

results.finding: The amplified random-language function distribution has negligible inversion success below T^(2−ε) wires.
results.detail: The construction uses log₂ λ parallel instances with independent prefix-defined random languages. The unamplified construction gives an inverse-polynomial bound.
results.quote:
For any
\(\varepsilon > 0\)
, there exists a
\((\textsf{negl}(\lambda ), 1-\varepsilon )\)
-fine-grained one-way function distribution in the random language model.

results.finding: Tiling Expansion is one-way iff any one-way function exists. The proof uses an n²-step simulation cutoff. Sample size is inapplicable.
results.detail: Section 3 measures randomized inversion on random inputs using Las Vegas algorithms. A polynomial-time inverter fits this framework by checking its answer and aborting on failure.
results.quote: Tiling Expansion is a owf if and only if owfs exist.

results.finding: One-way functions exist iff exact Kᵗ has error at least 1/p(n) for every PPT algorithm on uniform n-bit inputs, for every admissible t. Sample size is inapplicable.
results.detail: The source is a peer-reviewed IEEE FOCS proceedings paper. The schema has no conference category, so it is coded as report, with peer_reviewed reserved for journal papers.
results.quote:
In fact, our main theorem is stronger than stated: we
show that for every polynomial t(n) ≥ (1+ ε)n, where
ε> 0 is a constant, mild average-case hardness of Kt
is equivalent to the existence of one-way functions.
